items.questionText: Amy reads a sentence and it doesn't sound right. What should she do first? A) Skip the sentence   B) Stop and reread the sentence   C) Close the book
items.answerKey: Stop and reread the sentence
stepByStepSolution: Notice that the sentence sounded odd or didn't make sense.
Stop reading instead of guessing or skipping.
Go back and reread the sentence carefully.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking it's fine to keep going even when a sentence sounds wrong.
Skipping the tricky part instead of checking it.
hints: Good readers pause when something feels off.
The best first step is to go back, not push forward.

items.questionText: What is it called when you notice a mistake while reading and fix it yourself? A) Self-correcting   B) Scanning   C) Guessing
items.answerKey: Self-correcting
stepByStepSolution: A good reader notices when their reading sounds wrong.
They stop and fix the word or sentence themselves.
This fixing-it-yourself habit is called self-correcting.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking self-correcting means asking someone else to fix it.
Confusing self-correcting with simply reading faster.
hints: It's about noticing your OWN mistake.
The word starts with 'self-' because YOU fix it.

items.questionText: Tom read: 'The dog ran to the shop and bought some bones.' Tom stopped and said, 'Wait, dogs can't buy things!' What reading strategy is Tom using?
stepByStepSolution: Tom noticed the sentence didn't make sense.
He stopped reading to think about it.
This checking and fixing is a self-correction strategy.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking Tom made a mistake by stopping to think.
Believing good readers never question what they read.
hints: Tom realised something was wrong with the meaning.
This is the same strategy as 'checking it makes sense'.

items.questionText: Which sentence shows a reader using self-correction? A) 'I read the whole page without stopping.'   B) 'I read "form" but then reread it as "from" because that made more sense.'   C) 'I skipped the hard word and kept going.'
items.answerKey: 'I read "form" but then reread it as "from" because that made more sense.'
stepByStepSolution: Look for a reader noticing an error.
Check if they went back and fixed it themselves.
Option B shows noticing 'form' was wrong and fixing it to 'from'.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking skipping a hard word counts as self-correcting.
Believing reading without stopping is always the best approach.
hints: Self-correction always involves going BACK to fix something.
Look for the option where the reader changes a word after rereading.

items.questionText: Name one thing a good reader checks when a sentence doesn't sound right.
stepByStepSolution: A good reader pauses when a sentence feels wrong.
They ask themselves if it makes sense or sounds right.
If not, they reread to fix it.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking only spelling matters, not meaning.
Believing it's fine to ignore a sentence that sounds odd.
hints: Think about what a reader is trying to understand.
The answer relates to meaning or how it sounds.

items.questionText: When reading an instruction (procedural) text like a recipe, why is it important to read carefully and reread if unsure? A) Because missing a step could change the result   B) Because instructions are always boring   C) Because pictures are not allowed
items.answerKey: Because missing a step could change the result
stepByStepSolution: Procedural texts have steps that must be followed in order.
Missing or misreading a step can change the outcome.
Rereading carefully helps you follow steps correctly.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking all texts can be read the same way regardless of purpose.
Believing skipping a step in instructions doesn't matter.
hints: Think about what happens if you get a recipe step wrong.
The correct answer is about accuracy mattering for the result.

items.questionText: Jack reads 'The cat sat on the mat' but says 'The cat sad on the mat'. What should Jack do to fix this?
answerKey: go back and read it again
stepByStepSolution: Jack's sentence 'sad' doesn't make sense in that spot.
He should notice this and pause.
Then he should reread the sentence carefully to fix it.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking it's fine to keep reading with the wrong word.
Believing the meaning doesn't matter if the sentence still has words.
hints: Think about what a reader does when a word sounds wrong.
The answer is to go back and read it again.

items.questionText: Which strategy would help most when reading a non-fiction text with unfamiliar words, such as a book about space? A) Skip every hard word without checking meaning   B) Use headings, pictures and captions to help understand new words   C) Only read the title
items.answerKey: Use headings, pictures and captions to help understand new words
stepByStepSolution: Non-fiction texts often have headings, pictures and captions.
These features give clues about unfamiliar words.
Using them helps the reader understand new vocabulary.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking pictures and headings are just decorations.
Believing skipping unfamiliar words is always fine.
hints: Non-fiction texts have special features that help readers.
The best answer uses these features to work out meaning.

items.questionText: Explain why rereading a tricky sentence can help a reader understand a story better.
answerKey: it helps the reader check the meaning
it helps you understand what is happening
stepByStepSolution: Sometimes a sentence is tricky the first time you read it.
Rereading gives your brain another chance to work out the meaning.
This helps you understand the story more clearly.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking rereading is only for readers who aren't good at reading.
Believing understanding always happens on the first try.
hints: Think about what happens the second time you read something tricky.
The answer relates to clearing up confusion or checking meaning.

items.questionText: A reader notices a sentence doesn't make sense and thinks the word might be wrong. What is the BEST next step? A) Keep reading and ignore it   B) Look at the word again and check if another word would make more sense   C) Stop reading the whole book
items.answerKey: Look at the word again and check if another word would make more sense
stepByStepSolution: The reader has noticed a possible mistake.
The best step is to look again, not ignore it or give up.
Checking for a word that makes more sense fixes the confusion.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking ignoring the problem is easier and fine.
Believing one mistake means you should stop reading altogether.
hints: The best readers don't give up or ignore problems.
Look for the option where the reader checks and fixes the word.

items.questionText: What is the main problem in the story Ms Chen read? A) Ravi loses his lunch   B) Ravi's kite flies away   C) Ravi gets lost in the park
items.answerKey: Ravi's kite flies away
stepByStepSolution: Think about what event starts the story.
Ravi is chasing something through the park.
The problem is that his kite blows away.
commonMisconceptions: Mixing up small details, like thinking the problem was about lunch.
Forgetting the main event and focusing on a small detail instead.
hints: The title of the story is a big clue.
The problem is about something in the sky.

items.questionText: Which of these is a subordinating conjunction? A) because   B) and   C) but
items.answerKey: because
stepByStepSolution: A subordinating conjunction joins a main idea to a dependent idea.
'Because' shows a reason and joins two ideas this way.
'And' and 'but' are coordinating conjunctions instead.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking 'and' and 'but' are subordinating conjunctions.
Believing any joining word is a subordinating conjunction.
hints: Think about words like 'although' or 'since' - which option matches?
'Because' explains a reason for something.

items.questionText: Complete the sentence: 'We stayed inside ___ it was raining.'
stepByStepSolution: The sentence needs a word that gives a reason.
'It was raining' explains WHY they stayed inside.
'Because' or 'since' both correctly show this reason.
commonMisconceptions: Using 'and' instead of a subordinating conjunction.
Forgetting the missing word should explain a reason.
hints: Think about a word that means 'for this reason'.
It starts with 'b' or 's'.

items.questionText: Which sentence is a complex sentence? A) I like dogs and cats.   B) Although it was cold, we went to the beach.   C) The dog barked loudly.
items.answerKey: Although it was cold, we went to the beach.
stepByStepSolution: A complex sentence has a main idea and a dependent idea joined by a subordinating conjunction.
Look for a sentence starting with a word like 'although'.
Option B joins two ideas using 'although'.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking any sentence with 'and' is complex.
Believing a short simple sentence counts as complex.
hints: Look for a subordinating conjunction like 'although'.
The answer has two connected ideas.

items.questionText: Which sentence correctly joins the two ideas using 'although'? A) Although the test was hard, Maria passed it.   B) Maria passed it although the test was hard because.   C) The test was hard, Maria passed it although.
items.answerKey: Although the test was hard, Maria passed it.
stepByStepSolution: 'Although' should introduce the first idea, with a comma after it.
Check that the sentence reads smoothly and makes sense.
Option A correctly starts with 'Although' and uses a comma.
commonMisconceptions: Placing 'although' at the end in a confusing way.
Forgetting the comma after the 'although' clause.
hints: The word 'although' usually starts the sentence here.
Check where the comma should go.

items.questionText: Which subordinating conjunction best completes: 'She packed an umbrella ___ it might rain.' A) because   B) although   C) but
items.answerKey: because
stepByStepSolution: The sentence explains WHY she packed an umbrella.
'Because' shows the reason for her action.
'Although' and 'but' don't fit the reason being given.
commonMisconceptions: Choosing 'although', which shows contrast, not reason.
Thinking 'but' can join a main and dependent clause.
hints: Think about why she packed the umbrella.
The word should explain a reason.

items.questionText: Which subordinating conjunction means 'at the same time as'?
stepByStepSolution: Some conjunctions show reason, and some show time.
'While' is used to show two things happening together.
This makes it the correct answer for 'at the same time as'.
commonMisconceptions: Confusing 'while' with 'because', which shows reason.
Thinking 'if' means 'at the same time'.
hints: Think of a word used when two things happen together.
It rhymes with 'smile'.

items.questionText: Which sentence uses 'since' to show a reason (not time)? A) Since Monday, I have been sick.   B) Since it was her birthday, we baked a cake.   C) I have lived here since I was five.
items.answerKey: Since it was her birthday, we baked a cake.
stepByStepSolution: 'Since' can show either time or reason.
Check which sentence explains WHY something happened.
Option B explains the reason for baking a cake.
commonMisconceptions: Thinking 'since' always refers to time.
Missing that reason-based 'since' can be replaced with 'because'.
hints: Try replacing 'since' with 'because' in each sentence.
Only one sentence still makes sense with 'because'.

items.questionText: Which complex sentence is punctuated correctly? A) Although, it was late we kept playing.   B) Although it was late, we kept playing.   C) Although it was late we kept, playing.
items.answerKey: Although it was late, we kept playing.
stepByStepSolution: When the subordinating clause comes first, it needs a comma after it.
Check where the comma is placed in each option.
Option B places the comma correctly after 'late'.
commonMisconceptions: Putting a comma right after 'Although'.
Placing the comma in the wrong spot in the main clause.
hints: The comma should come after the whole 'although' clause.
Only one option has the comma in the right place.

items.questionText: Which sentence correctly combines the ideas using 'if'? A) If you finish your homework, you can watch TV.   B) You can watch if TV you finish your homework.   C) If, you can watch TV finish your homework.
items.answerKey: If you finish your homework, you can watch TV.
stepByStepSolution: 'If' introduces a condition and usually starts the sentence.
Check that the sentence reads clearly and makes sense.
Option A correctly places 'if' at the start with a comma.
commonMisconceptions: Placing 'if' in the middle in a confusing way.
Forgetting the comma after the 'if' clause.
hints: 'If' should introduce the condition clearly.
Read each option aloud to see which makes sense.

items.questionText: Which sentence has the subordinating conjunction placed correctly to start the sentence? A) Because I was tired, I went to bed early.   B) I because was tired went to bed early.   C) I went to bed early because, I was tired.
items.answerKey: Because I was tired, I went to bed early.
stepByStepSolution: A subordinating conjunction can start a sentence if followed by a comma later.
Check that the sentence reads smoothly.
Option A places 'because' correctly at the start with a comma after the clause.
commonMisconceptions: Putting the conjunction in the middle of a clause awkwardly.
Adding an unnecessary comma right after 'because'.
hints: 'Because' should start the whole first idea.
The comma comes after the reason, not right after 'because'.

items.questionText: What is Text 1 mainly about? A) An ant who works hard and prepares for winter   B) A grasshopper who becomes a farmer   C) A seed that grows into a sunflower
items.answerKey: An ant who works hard and prepares for winter
stepByStepSolution: Text 1 follows Ana the ant through summer and winter.
She works hard collecting and storing seeds.
This shows the text is mainly about preparing for winter.
commonMisconceptions: Mixing up the ant story with the seed story.
Focusing on Grady instead of the main character, Ana.
hints: Think about which character does the most in Text 1.
The main idea is about preparing ahead of time.
items.passage:
Text 1: The Busy Ant
All summer, Ana the ant worked hard collecting seeds and storing them in her underground nest. Her friend Grady the grasshopper spent his days singing in the sun instead of gathering food. When winter came, Ana had plenty of food stored away, while Grady had nothing to eat. Ana kindly shared some of her seeds with Grady and reminded him gently that planning ahead helps in tough times.

Text 2: The Patient Seed
Priya planted a sunflower seed in a small pot on her windowsill. Every day she watered it and checked for sunlight, but for over a week, nothing happened. Her older brother said the seed might never grow. Priya kept caring for it patiently anyway. On the twelfth day, a tiny green shoot finally poked through the soil. Priya's patience had paid off, and she felt proud of what she had grown.
